meta.h1: The Winning Paper: what takes an award entry from good to great
meta.byline: 3 October 2026 · Sam · AI researcher, Run with Foxes

intro.p: I've spent this week inside other people's award papers. With a team of AI agents I read 470 of them, each one from start to end. The largest set runs to 1.6 million words, and we read most of it more than once. That made 1,032 full readings and 4.4 million words.

We put the same questions to every paper, up to 67 of them. Does it state an insight? Does it say what would have happened without the campaign? Does it show profit, or only revenue? That gave us 23,902 answers. For most of them we copied out the sentence in the paper that the answer rests on, which came to 5,713 passages. We counted 969 objectives and 6,320 charts. And we logged 1,599 separate times that an author named something else that might have caused their own result.
I did all of that because I wanted to know one thing. When two decent pieces of work go in for the same award, why is one awarded and the other isn't?
intro.hl: I did all of that because I wanted to know one thing. When two decent pieces of work go in for the same award, why is one awarded and the other isn't?

intro.p: I thought the answer would be the story. I expected the awarded papers to have the insight and the others to be missing it. That isn't what the counts show. Nearly every paper has an insight, a diagnosis and a strategy that follows from it. Those are table stakes. Sales rising while a campaign runs is correlation. What the awarded papers add is proof of causation: that the work caused the result.
So if you've been asked to write an award entry, this report is for you. It shows what the awarded papers do on top of the basics, with the counts, so you can take your own entry from good to great.

Of the 470 papers, 389 are from Paul Dervan's own archive, collected over the past 20 years and reaching back to 1980. The other 81 are Irish winners that anyone can open: 40 from the Effie Awards Ireland and 41 from ADFX. We also read the entry rules of 9 award bodies, in their own published guides.

intro.title: What we read
intro.cap: Every paper was read from start to end by an AI agent working to a written list of questions. The agents were not told which papers had been awarded.

intro.p: The comparison at the centre of this report uses 190 of those papers. They come from one long-running effectiveness award, in the nine years where the archive holds both sides: 103 papers that were awarded and 87 that were entered and not awarded. Same award, same years, same rules.
Anything entered for an award like this is already decent work. So the differences below are differences in how the paper was written.

findings.text: Insight is table stakes. 99% of awarded papers state one, and so do 93% of the others (102 of 103 and 81 of 87). The same goes for a diagnosis, a strategy that answers it and a story told in order. You need them, and a paper without them stands out for the wrong reason. They get you to good (Chapter 1).

Great starts with proof of causation. 84% of awarded papers give a figure for what would have happened anyway, against 53% of the others (87 of 103 and 46 of 87). 83% use a model or a control test, against 46% (85 and 40). These are two of the three widest gaps we found, and the third is about proof too (Chapter 2).
Awarded papers come back to where they started. 92% show that the thing they said was wrong has changed, against 80% (95 of 103 and 70 of 87) (Chapter 3).
They give it time. 81% show their measure over three years or more, against 56% (83 of 103 and 49 of 87) (Chapter 4).
They show the payback. 69% make a profit claim, against 41% (71 of 103 and 36 of 87). No awarded paper left payback out, and 14% of the others did (12 of 87) (Chapter 5).
The scoring says the same thing in advance. Wherever an award body publishes its weights, results get the most points (Chapter 6).
The best papers teach a way of thinking, and none of it needs a bigger budget (Chapter 7).

lede.p: Insights matter. So does a diagnosis, and a strategy that follows from it, and a story that runs in order. They matter so much that nearly every paper in the archive has them, awarded or not. That is what table stakes means. You can't sit down without them.

blocks.p: Figure 1.1 takes six things a well-built paper has and counts them in both groups.

blocks.alt: Bar chart. States an insight: 99% and 93%; Whole case in the first 300 words: 87% and 83%; States a commercial objective: 85% and 86%; Diagnosis names a cause: 96% and 98%; Says why the strategy answers it: 97% and 98%; Order: problem, strategy, results: 86% and 87%
blocks.title: The table stakes. Nearly every paper has them
blocks.cap: Share of papers. Insight: 102 of 103 awarded, 81 of 87 not awarded. Whole case in the first 300 words: 90 of 103 awarded, 72 of 87 not awarded. Commercial objective: 88 of 103 awarded, 75 of 87 not awarded. A diagnosis that names a cause: 99 of 103 awarded, 85 of 87 not awarded. Says why the strategy answers it: 100 of 103 awarded, 85 of 87 not awarded. Order runs problem, strategy, results: 89 of 103 awarded, 76 of 87 not awarded.

blocks.p: Read that chart the right way round. It doesn't say these things are unimportant. It says they are so important that almost nobody enters without them. Only 1 awarded paper in 103 has no stated insight. If yours is missing one of these, a judge will notice, and it's a flag. So start here, and get them right. Then go on, because having them puts you level with everyone else. The rest of this report is about what takes a paper from there to great.

Since an insight is something you can't enter without, it's worth being sure yours is one. The forms ask for it, and only one award body says what it means. The Effie entry kit asks for "INSIGHTS- not just facts or observations, but what came out from the data points/research". Its jury tips add that a data point isn't an insight, and neither is your objective said again.

We gave that definition to two AI agents and asked each one to judge the 40 public Effie Ireland winners on its own. They agreed on 30. If two agents with the definition in front of them disagree on a quarter of the papers, a writer on a deadline will too. So use a test you can apply: is it about people, is it about these people and this brand, and did the idea come from it?

lede.p: Sales went up while the campaign ran. That is correlation. It tells you the two things happened together. It doesn't tell you the campaign caused the rise, because a price cut, wider distribution, good weather or a rival's bad year could have done the same. Showing causation is the widest difference in everything we read.

blocks.p: Figure 2.1 takes five ways a paper can show causation. For each one it gives the share of awarded papers that do it and the share of the others. Look at the gap between the two groups in each row. These are the widest gaps in the report.

blocks.alt: Bar chart. A figure for what would have happened anyway: 84% and 53%; Headline is what the activity added: 61% and 39%; A model or a control test: 83% and 46%; Rules out 3+ other causes with a figure: 78% and 45%; A number at each step, work to sale: 95% and 68%
blocks.title: Awarded papers say what would have happened without the work
blocks.cap: Share of papers. Gives a figure for what would have happened anyway: 87 of 103 awarded, 46 of 87 not awarded. Headline result is what the activity added, not the total rise: 63 of 103 awarded, 34 of 87 not awarded. Uses a model or a control test: 85 of 103 awarded, 40 of 87 not awarded. Rules out three or more other causes with a figure: 80 of 103 awarded, 39 of 87 not awarded. Shows each step from the work to the sale with a number: 98 of 103 awarded, 59 of 87 not awarded.

blocks.p: Nearly half of the papers that weren't awarded never say what sales would have been without the activity. That figure has a name, the counterfactual, and it is the plainest test of causation there is. More than half of those papers lead with the total rise and credit the campaign for all of it. The awarded papers lead with the incremental part, which is what the campaign added.

Across the 389 archive papers, the authors named another possible cause of their own result 1,599 times. They named price, promotions, distribution, the market, competitors, the season, the weather and product changes. In 1,023 of those they answered with a figure, a chart or a named source. In 576 they answered with a sentence.
The middle awarded paper names 6 other causes and rules out 4 with data. The middle paper that wasn't awarded names 4 and rules out 2. Most teams already hold the data to close that gap.

subs.title: What you can still fix, and what you can't

blocks.p: Two rows in Figure 2.1 are decided long before anyone writes. If nobody built an econometric model and no region was held back as a control, no paragraph can supply one. Say so early and plainly. Then build the best comparison you have. That could be a forecast made before the activity, the market, a close rival, or a period or a place without the work.

The other three are within any writer's reach. Put a figure against each other cause. State what the activity added and not the total. Show the number at each step: people saw it, it changed what they thought or did, and sales moved.

blocks.held: A public Irish paper that does this well, named by brand and year, once it has been opened and checked. Two candidates from the Effie Ireland booklets: the paper that says plainly it cannot separate the campaign's effect, and the one that credits the public.
blocks.label: Held for Paul

lede.p: Here is where the story itself goes from good to great. Every paper starts well. The great ones come back to where they started.

subs.title: Did the thing you diagnosed change?

blocks.p: Figure 3.1 puts two things side by side. The first is whether a paper says what was wrong. The second is whether its results show that same thing changing. Look at how close the two groups are on the first, and how they part on the second.

blocks.alt: Bar chart. States a diagnosis that names a cause: 96% and 98%; Results show the diagnosed problem changed: 92% and 80%
blocks.title: Nearly every paper makes a diagnosis. Awarded papers return to it
blocks.cap: Share of papers. States a diagnosis that names a cause: 99 of 103 awarded, 85 of 87 not awarded. The results show that the diagnosed problem changed: 95 of 103 awarded, 70 of 87 not awarded.

blocks.p: The usual gap looks like this. A paper says the problem was how people saw the brand. Then its results report sales. Sales may well have risen. But the paper said the cause was a belief, so a judge will want to see the belief move.

The test takes two minutes. Write your diagnosis in one sentence. Then find the chart in your results that shows that exact thing changing. If it isn't there, find it, or say that you couldn't measure it.

blocks.held: Paul's own account of what a strong story does, from judging: diagnosis, to strategy, to results.
blocks.label: Held for Paul

lede.p: A result measured against last year tells a judge little, because last year might have been a bad one. A line that runs back several years shows whether this is a real change or an ordinary wobble.

subs.title: What the result is compared with

blocks.p: Figure 4.1 looks at what a paper compares its result with, and how far back it looks. The first two rows are the stronger comparisons, and the rows below them are weaker. Look at which group does each one more often.

blocks.alt: Bar chart. Shows the measure over 3+ years: 81% and 56%; Compares with a forecast, model or control: 48% and 33%; Compares with the previous year: 28% and 36%; Compares with a target, the market or nothing: 9% and 18%; Shows no history before the activity: 10% and 21%; Compares with the previous 6 months or less: 2% and 8%
blocks.title: Awarded papers show a longer line and compare against a baseline
blocks.cap: Share of papers. Shows the measure over three years or more: 83 of 103 awarded, 49 of 87 not awarded. Shows no history before the activity: 10 of 103 awarded, 18 of 87 not awarded. Main comparison is a forecast, a model or a control: 49 of 103 awarded, 29 of 87 not awarded. Main comparison is the previous year: 29 of 103 awarded, 31 of 87 not awarded. Main comparison is a target, the market alone, or nothing: 9 of 103 awarded, 16 of 87 not awarded. Main comparison is the previous six months or less: 2 of 103 awarded, 7 of 87 not awarded.

blocks.p: Figure 4.2 counts how long the results run after the activity began. It runs from one year to five. Look at how the gap between the two groups holds as the stretch gets longer.

blocks.alt: Bar chart. A year or more: 78% and 61%; Two years or more: 48% and 30%; Three years or more: 36% and 20%; Five years or more: 16% and 8%
blocks.title: Awarded papers report results for longer
blocks.cap: Share of papers reporting results for at least this long after the activity began. A year: 80 of 103 awarded, 53 of 87 not awarded. Two years: 49 and 26. Three years: 37 and 17. Five years: 16 and 7. Six months or less: 15 awarded, 25 not awarded.

blocks.p: The middle awarded paper reports 20 months of results. The middle paper that wasn't awarded reports 12.

I'd like to tell you that five years of history is the mark of an awarded paper. I can't. 29 of 103 awarded papers show five years or more before the activity, and so do 23 of 87 of the others. The middle paper in both groups shows three. What separates them is showing a long line at all, and comparing against a baseline such as a forecast or a control.

blocks.held: Paul's view, from judging, that a comparison over five years is stronger than one over six months or a year. The papers support the direction. They can't prove the five.
blocks.label: Held for Paul

lede.p: Revenue isn't profit. A return worked out on revenue isn't a return on investment. It's the oldest note in the judges' guides, and it still separates the papers.

blocks.p: Figure 5.1 sorts the papers by how they report payback. The first two are profit. The third is revenue on its own. The last is no payback at all. Look at the last one first.

blocks.alt: Bar chart. Makes a profit claim: 69% and 41%; Shows net profit with the sum: 42% and 23%; Gives a revenue return only: 18% and 33%; Gives no payback at all: 0% and 14%
blocks.title: No awarded paper left payback out
blocks.cap: Share of papers. Makes a profit claim: 71 of 103 awarded, 36 of 87 not awarded. Shows net profit with the sum: 43 of 103 awarded, 20 of 87 not awarded. Gives a revenue return only: 19 of 103 awarded, 29 of 87 not awarded. Gives no payback at all: 0 of 103 awarded, 12 of 87 not awarded.

blocks.p: Say what margin you used and where it came from. Take the cost of the activity off. Show the sum. If the figures are confidential, both the IPA and the Effies let you show them as an index.

subs.title: Payback in the public Irish papers

blocks.p: In the public Irish papers, payback stated as profit is rare. Of 41 ADFX papers, 6 state payback as profit. Of 40 Effie Ireland winners, about 8 or 9 claim a return and none states profit.

subs.title: Put a source on every figure

blocks.p: Result figures with no source appear in 10 of the 103 awarded papers and 32 of the 87 others. Awarded papers are edited before they're printed, which may explain part of that. The Effie rules disqualify unsourced data. It's the cheapest thing in this report to fix.

chapters.title: Read the scoring before you write

lede.p: Everything above is in the entry guides, if you read them as a judge would. Count the points before you count your words.

blocks.p: Figure 6.1 sets out how four award bodies score an entry, in the words of their own guides. Look at which part of the entry gets the most points in each one.

blocks.title: Wherever weights are published, results get the most points
blocks.cap: From each body's own published guide. We read 94 entry questions and judging criteria across 9 bodies. ADFX is left out: the guides we could reach are archived, from 2014 to 2018, and the current kit should be read before anything is said about it.

blocks.p: The IPA's pack says the results section "should take up about 50% of the paper if not more". It says you should be able to put the whole argument "in one paragraph, or better yet, in one sentence", with one chart that shows it.

In the papers we read, the middle awarded paper gives 45% of its words to results and proof. The middle paper that wasn't awarded gives 35%. 37 of 103 awarded papers give more than half, against 16 of 87.

chapters.title: What the best papers teach about thinking

lede.p: This is the chapter I didn't plan. I expected the strongest papers to claim the most. They claim less, and then they make it stick. We asked the agents to write one line on what each paper teaches about clear thinking. That gave me 389 lines. I read all of them, and the same habits kept coming back.
They rule out the other causes one at a time, each with its own answer.

They say what they can't prove, and narrow the claim to what they can. One paper campaigned for a change in the law, and the law changed. The authors could have claimed it. They wrote that the law might have passed anyway, claimed only that it came sooner, and built their payback on that smaller claim. One limits its claim to the weeks when the advertising was the only reason anyone had to call. One says plainly that it has no model, and asks only how small a share of the rise would have to be the campaign's for it to pay for itself. In the comparison, 92 of 103 awarded papers admit a limit or something that didn't work, and 68 of 87 of the others do too. It's common. It's safe. Judges read it as strength.
They set the targets first and report against each one, including the ones they missed.

They find a fair comparison. One holds a region quiet. One uses the markets that didn't run the work. One uses a rival on the same network, and one uses the products in its own range that weren't advertised. One counts the same 250 stores throughout, so new openings don't flatter the number.

They separate the real problem from the brief. They show the routes that failed, and what each one changed. They build their sums to be cautious: the lowest margin, a low and a high figure, and in one paper a return the authors cut by 60% themselves.

None of this needs a bigger budget. It's a way of thinking about your own work. A team that can write down what was wrong, why this was the answer, what would have happened anyway and what it paid back understands its work better than a team that can't. That's true whether or not the paper is ever entered. I think it's the best reason to write one.

lede.held: Paul on what he has learned from reading brilliant cases: their clarity of thinking and their rigour, in his own words. And what the papers can't show: what he saw in the judging room.
lede.label: Held for Paul

method.t: 389 award papers from Paul Dervan's archive, 1980 to 2024, 342 of them from 2006 on. They are what one person collected over the years, not every paper entered. 40 Effie Awards Ireland winners from the 2021 and 2023 case study booklets, and 41 ADFX papers from 2012 to 2018, are public and were read in full.

Each paper was read from start to end by an AI agent working to a written list of questions: 32 questions on how the paper is built and proved, 16 on diagnosis, cause and time frames, and 19 on the strategy. That made 1,032 full readings and 23,902 recorded answers. For most answers the agent copied out the sentence it rests on, 5,713 passages in all, so any answer can be checked against the paper.
For the comparison, the prize was taken off each paper before it was read. 11 papers name their own prize in their opening lines, so the agent was not blind on those.

In each of the first two passes, 32 papers were read a second time by a different agent working on its own. On every count used in this report the two agents agreed on 27 to 32 of the 32. One question was dropped because the agents took it two ways.
103 awarded and 87 not awarded papers from the same award, 2010 to 2018, the only years where the archive holds both. "Not awarded" is the label on the file; some may have been shortlisted.

The agents saw each paper's text and not its chart images. Anything that sits only in a chart was missed. For that reason we don't report which result a paper leads with, or whether its objective had a target number.

Percentages are rounded to the nearest whole number. Where a chart prints a gap in points, it is the difference between the two rounded percentages, so it matches what you see on the chart. Worked out from the counts, six of those gaps would be one point different.

Awarded papers are edited before they're printed. The others are closer to what was submitted. That may explain some of the difference in sourcing. It can't add a model or a control test, and the main differences hold when papers in the same printed form are compared.
It shows what awarded papers contain. It doesn't show that any one of these things wins an award. Brands with the budget for a model may also have had the stronger work.

We've also read every paper for the problem the brand had and the move it made, by category. That map needs a second read before we publish a number from it. And we're building a coach that works through all of this with a writer, one question at a time. I haven't figured out yet how to make it ask about charts.
